171.quote_or_event: “Taking anything that is not given is stealing (steya).” Pūjyapāda adds: “It follows that activity actuated by impure dispositions is stealing (steya), whether external objects are taken or not.”
171.explanation: The third Jain vow, asteya, forbids taking what is not given, and the standard commentary extends the fault inward: a passion-driven reaching for another's property is already theft, even before anything is seized.
171.tie_back: Valluvar says merely setting one's heart on another's property brings ruin and guilt at once, and the Jain commentary agrees that the covetous disposition itself counts as stealing.
171.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.15, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
171._accuracy_note: Both sentences verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a strong doctrinal fit on coveting as already culpable, though the kural's ruin of the family is not addressed.

172.quote_or_event: Queen Kamalāvatī to King Ishukāra: “A man who returns, as it were, to the vomit, is not praised; but you want to confiscate the property left by the Brâhmaṇa. If the whole world and all treasures were yours, you would still not be satisfied, nor would all this be able to save you.”
172.explanation: When the king prepares to seize the estate abandoned by the family that renounced the world, the queen shames him by likening such greed to eating vomit, and the king himself then renounces.
172.tie_back: Valluvar says those with a sense of shame at unfairness will not stoop to disgraceful acts for gain, and the queen's rebuke shows shame checking a king who was about to take another's property.
172._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong narrative fit for shame restraining a covetous act, though the property was legally escheatable (Jacobi's note), so the unfairness is moral rather than legal.

173.quote_or_event: “Pleasures bring only a moment's happiness, but suffering for a very long time, intense suffering, but slight happiness; they are an obstacle to the liberation from existence, and are a very mine of evils.”
173.explanation: The two sons of the priest Bhṛgu refuse their father's offer of wealth and pleasures, explaining that momentary enjoyment costs long suffering and blocks the lasting goal of liberation.
173.tie_back: Valluvar says those who seek the other, lasting joy will not do wrong for a petty, passing pleasure, and the Jain verse sets the same contrast between a moment's pleasure and the enduring good of liberation.
173._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a near one-to-one fit for petty pleasure set against lasting bliss (Parimelazhagar also reads the 'other joy' as heaven or liberation).

174.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means. Though two mâshas would do to supply your want, still you would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.”
174.explanation: In the commentary's frame story, the poor student Kapila set out to earn two pieces of gold; offered any wish by the king, he kept raising his demand until he saw what was happening, renounced on the spot and spoke this verse.
174.tie_back: Valluvar says those who have mastered their senses will not covet others' goods even when they think 'we have nothing', and Kapila, a needy man, saw through his own rising craving and gave it up.
174.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 8.17, with Jacobi's note summarizing the commentary's story of Kapila (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
174._accuracy_note: Verse verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com and the story checked against Jacobi's footnote there; a strong fit for poverty not excusing craving, though Kapila wanted a gift offered to him, not another person's goods.

175.quote_or_event: “Knowledge without right conduct, acceptance of the asceticism without right faith and observance of austerities without self-control are all futile.”
175.explanation: Jainism's three jewels must go together: learning that is not joined to right conduct does not lead to liberation and is counted worthless.
175.tie_back: Valluvar asks what use a deep and wide intellect is if its owner covets others' goods and acts senselessly, and the Jain verse likewise calls knowledge without right conduct futile.
175.source: Saman Suttam, verse 210 (Ratnatrayasutra; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
175._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Saman Suttam English text on jainworld.com; a strong match on knowledge being worthless without conduct, but the verse does not name covetousness.

176.quote_or_event: “When suppressed, passion can bring about the spiritual degeneration of even the most virtuous monk, who in his conduct is akin to Jina himself, what can we say of monks who are under the sway of attachment?”
176.explanation: Jain teaching warns that passions (kaṣāya), greed among them, merely held down rather than destroyed can bring down even a monk whose conduct resembles a Jina's.
176.tie_back: Valluvar says even one who has longed for grace and stood on virtue's path will be ruined once he covets others' wealth, and the Jain verse warns that passion can make even the most virtuous fall.
176.source: Saman Suttam, verse 132 (Samyamasutra; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
176._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com; a strong fit for the fall of the advanced practitioner, though it speaks of passions in general rather than coveting wealth.

177.quote_or_event: “Pleasures are the thorn that rankles, pleasures are poison, pleasures are like a venomous snake; he who is desirous of pleasures will not get them, and will come to a bad end at last.”
177.explanation: King Nami tells Indra, who has urged him to multiply his gold and treasury, that grasping after objects of desire ends badly however good it looks at first.
177.tie_back: Valluvar says gain born of coveting will rarely ripen into good fruit, and Nami likewise says the one who covets pleasures comes to a bad end at last.
177._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable fit on the bad final outcome of covetous desire, but it concerns pleasures generally rather than gain taken from others.

178.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.” And: “One ought to put an end to anger through calmness, pride by modesty, deceit by straight-forwardness and greed by contentment.”
178.explanation: This Saman Suttam couplet (a rendering of Daśavaikālika 8.38) ranks greed as the passion that ruins everything, and prescribes contentment (santoṣa) as its cure.
178.tie_back: Valluvar says the way to keep one's wealth from dwindling is not to covet another's, and the Jain verses agree that greed destroys everything while contentment overcomes it.
178.source: Saman Suttam, verses 135–136 (Samyamasutra; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com); cf. Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.38
178._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com; the claim that greed destroys and contentment protects fits, but the verses do not promise that one's own wealth will be preserved, which is the kural's point.

179.quote_or_event: After King Nami refused to multiply his treasury, Śakra (Indra) dropped his disguise and praised him: “Bravo! you have conquered anger; bravo! you have vanquished pride; bravo! you have banished delusion; bravo! you have subdued greed.”
179.explanation: The king of the gods, who had tested Nami by urging wealth and conquest on him, comes in his true form to honour the one who desired nothing, then pays him reverence and departs.
179.tie_back: Valluvar pictures Fortune seeking out the wise who do not covet, and in the Jain story it is the king of gods himself who comes to honour the sage who has subdued greed.
179._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial fit, since Śakra brings praise, not prosperity, and Jainism has no fortune-goddess who rewards virtue (results follow from karma).

180.quote_or_event: “Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself.”
180.explanation: Asked by Indra to subdue rival princes, King Nami replies that victory over one's own self, including the greed he goes on to name, is greater than any outward conquest.
180.tie_back: Valluvar ends by saying that the proud strength of not wanting gives birth to victory, and Nami's teaching names that very self-mastery the greatest victory.
180._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong fit for non-desire as true victory, though the verse concerns self-conquest broadly and does not mention the ruin that coveting brings (the kural's other half).
